content: We are delighted and privileged to extend our congratulations to the Council to Improve Foodborne Outbreak Response (CIFOR) on the publication of its groundbreaking Guidelines for Foodborne Disease Outbreak Response. These guidelines address critical components of a more effective, prevention-focused food safety system. The document represents the culmination of a three-year collaborative effort involving public health and food safety professionals and experts from all levels of government. This collaboration aimed to enhance our response to foodborne outbreaks and establish a unified framework for evaluating foodborne disease surveillance. The CIFOR process itself serves as a model for the type of cross-disciplinary, interagency, and interjurisdictional collaboration necessary to address complex issues like foodborne illness, which transcend traditional boundaries. The publication of these guidelines is also significant because it reflects a commitment to harmonizing and integrating the detection, investigation, and control of outbreaks by health officials and regulators, ultimately reducing the number of people who become ill. By standardizing data collection, improving data sharing, and fostering new levels and methods of collaboration, we have the opportunity not only to contain outbreaks more rapidly but also to derive valuable lessons for future prevention efforts. However, like any set of guidelines, the ultimate success of the Guidelines for Foodborne Disease Outbreak Response depends on their implementation by our colleagues in local, state, and federal agencies. These guidelines provide both a flexible, forward-looking framework and a call to action. This call to action is equally important in the policy arena. Implementing the guidelines requires the commitment of policymakers and elected officials, who, as representatives of the public, rightly demand improved foodborne disease surveillance and outbreak response. These officials must also provide the legal authority, financial resources, and organizational capacity necessary to achieve these goals. The CIFOR guidelines point the way toward a more robust system for outbreak response. The CIFOR guidelines were developed to assist government agencies responsible for preventing and managing foodborne diseases. They focus on local and state agencies, including public health, environmental health, agriculture, and other food safety-related entities, as these agencies investigate the majority of foodborne disease outbreaks in the United States. The guidelines outline the overall approach to foodborne disease outbreaks, including preparation, detection, investigation, control, and follow-up. They also define the roles of key organizations involved in these outbreaks, provide recommendations for improving communication and coordination among multiple agencies during multijurisdictional outbreaks, and identify performance indicators that organizations can use to evaluate their response efforts. Although the guidelines offer comprehensive information for individuals and organizations involved in foodborne disease response, they are not intended to replace existing procedural manuals. Instead, agencies and individuals should use the guidelines to compare existing procedures, address gaps, update site-specific protocols, create new procedures where none exist, and train program staff. CIFOR envisions these guidelines as a foundation for epidemiologists, laboratorians, environmental health specialists, and others involved in food safety programs. By standardizing foodborne disease investigations across agencies, CIFOR hopes to improve the consistency and effectiveness of outbreak responses. The guidelines were developed through the efforts of technical experts from various government and academic organizations across the country, representing a wide range of disciplines. The document underwent a comprehensive public review process and is considered a consensus document that captures best practices and identifies emerging approaches in foodborne disease outbreak response. The development of the CIFOR guidelines required thousands of hours of work by dozens of individuals over a three-year period. Many of these contributors balanced their full-time jobs with the demands of responding to foodborne disease outbreaks during the project. Their dedication to improving the quality of outbreak response is deeply appreciated. CIFOR extends its gratitude to all participants, with special acknowledgment to individuals like John Besser, Craig Hedberg, Pat McConnon, Don Sharp, and Jeanette Stehr-Green, who provided additional guidance and support as needed. Jac Davies, the editor and lead author, played a particularly significant role in the creation of this document, and her contributions are especially recognized. The organizations participating in CIFOR and their representatives contributed to the development of these guidelines. While various steps for investigating an outbreak exist in the training literature, there is no universally agreed-upon standard approach for outbreak response. This is because no single set of steps is appropriate for all outbreaks, as responses vary depending on factors such as the etiologic agent, the number of cases, the likely source of exposure, the agencies involved, available resources, and the expertise of investigators. Additionally, certain activities may be required by local ordinances or state statutes in some jurisdictions but not in others. The CIFOR guidelines provide a structured description of the steps involved in outbreak response, emphasizing the need for systematic investigation while allowing for flexibility in the order, magnitude, or necessity of associated activities. The guidelines also address the complexities of multijurisdictional outbreaks and provide special considerations for such scenarios. They cover fundamental concepts of public health surveillance and foodborne disease, legal considerations for surveillance and control, and performance indicators for assessing outbreak response efforts. The guidelines aim to improve planning and preparation, which are essential for identifying the source of an outbreak more quickly and implementing control measures more effectively. They emphasize the importance of pre-identified protocols, access to resources, and training for outbreak response teams. Agencies are encouraged to establish procedures for receiving and tracking complaints of potential foodborne illnesses, maintain updated contact lists, and develop policies for sharing information among team members and implicated facilities. Good communication is critical throughout the investigation of a foodborne disease outbreak. Agencies should establish protocols for actions required before implicated facilities or food sources can resume normal operations and create processes for after-action reports to document lessons learned and quality improvement measures. Legal preparedness is also a cornerstone of effective outbreak response, requiring appropriate laws, competent staff, and agreements for coordinated implementation across jurisdictions. In cases of multijurisdictional outbreaks or when resources are insufficient, investigators should escalate the investigation and involve other agencies promptly. The use of an Incident Command System (ICS) can facilitate internal and external communication and coordination during an outbreak response. The CIFOR guidelines represent a significant step forward in improving the consistency, efficiency, and effectiveness of foodborne disease outbreak response efforts.
